claim: As of 2025 there were more than 6.5 million podcasts, reaching nearly 600 million listeners worldwide.
quote: There are more than 6.5 million of them, and they reach nearly 600 million listeners worldwide.
speaker: Zachary Crockett (narration)
note: Episode-cited resource: 'Podcast Statistics You Need To Know' (Backlinko).

claim: Podcast (and TV/digital) ads are priced by CPM — cost per thousand impressions; the 'M' is the Roman numeral for 1,000. At a $25 CPM, an episode with 100,000 downloads earns $2,500 per ad.
quote: CPM stands for "cost per thousand," and Roman numeral M of thousand, so that's where it came from.
speaker: Gabe Tartaglia, VP of podcast & satellite monetization, SiriusXM
note: Tartaglia says observed CPMs range from $5 to $100 per 1,000 downloads.

claim: Podcast ad revenue rose 26% in the prior year — more than three times the growth rate of the digital-audio industry overall.
quote: Podcast ad revenue was up 26 percent last year — more than 3 times the growth for the digital audio industry at large.
speaker: Zachary Crockett (narration)
note: Episode-cited resource: IAB 'Digital Ad Revenue Surges 15% YoY in 2024' (2025).

claim: Podcast ad slots are named by position: pre-roll (start), mid-roll (middle), post-roll (end). Pre-roll runs ~20% cheaper than mid-roll; post-roll is nominal because few listeners reach the end.
quote: Pre-roll is typically about 20 percent cheaper than mid-roll, and then post-roll is, you know, very nominal.
speaker: Gabe Tartaglia, SiriusXM

claim: A typical 20-minute episode distills roughly 4 hours of recorded interview tape (2–3 guests, 60–90 min each) into a ~3,500-word script.
quote: we're collecting 4 hours of guest tape that we're going to boil down into an episode that's roughly 20 minutes.
speaker: Sarah Lilley, senior producer
note: Related figure from same episode: a 20-minute episode is ~3,500 words / ~10 pages.

claim: A 'tape sync' is when a local audio engineer travels to a remote guest with gear to capture studio-quality audio; it typically costs $300–$400, versus ~$150/hour for a booked studio.
quote: That is an audio engineer that will travel to the guest and they'll bring all the gear needed in order to connect to us for the interview.
speaker: Jeremy Johnston, audio engineer

claim: In the U.S., just 5% of the population accounts for 50% of annual healthcare spending.
quote: in the U.S., just five percent of the population accounts for 50 percent of annual healthcare spending.
speaker: Bapu Jena (host)

episode.title: What Can We Do About the Hardest Patients? (Replay)

note: Episode-cited resource: KFF Health System Tracker (2021).

claim: 'Super-utilizers' are patients with multiple chronic conditions (often plus mental-health, housing, and addiction challenges) who use hospitals repeatedly. In Camden NJ, the single leading utilizer averaged 113 hospital visits per year.
quote: The leading utilizer averaged 113 visits annually.
speaker: Bapu Jena (narration)

episode.title: What Can We Do About the Hardest Patients? (Replay)

note: Same episode: 2002–2007, 50% of Camden residents used an ER/hospital in a year — twice the national rate.

claim: 'Hot-spotting' borrows from policing — using data to find geographic/individual concentrations (of crime, or of costly patients) and target intervention there. The Camden Coalition applied it to super-utilizers.
quote: The term borrows from a policing strategy, where data is used to identify geographic locations that are hotspots for crime.
speaker: Bapu Jena (narration)

episode.title: What Can We Do About the Hardest Patients? (Replay)

note: Popularized by Atul Gawande, 'The Hot Spotters,' The New Yorker (2011).

claim: When you select people at an extreme (e.g. peak illness), they tend to improve on their own afterward — so a program can look effective in before/after data even if it does nothing. The Camden RCT found ~62% of BOTH treatment and control patients were readmitted within 6 months, with no difference between them.
quote: about 62 percent of both the treatment and the control group reentered the hospital.
speaker: Joseph Doyle, MIT economist

episode.title: What Can We Do About the Hardest Patients? (Replay)

note: Study: 'Health Care Hotspotting — A Randomized, Controlled Trial,' NEJM (2020).

headword: PACE (Program of All-Inclusive Care for the Elderly)
claim: PACE is a ~30-year-old, fully risk-capitated care model (originating in San Francisco) for nursing-home-eligible seniors, providing on-site primary care, therapy, transport, and full financial responsibility for the patient's care.
quote: PACE is a 30-year-old model — spread all over the country now — it started in San Francisco.
speaker: Jeffrey Brenner, founder of the Camden Coalition

episode.title: What Can We Do About the Hardest Patients? (Replay)
